Thank you to the thousands of citizens who stood up and spoke out about their serious concerns!
The Department of Health has notified us they are withdrawing Proposed Rulemaking – Communicable and Noncommunicable Diseases (#10-242 / IRRC # 3490) from consideration by the Independent Regulatory Review Commission on September 25, 2026.
The withdrawal of Gov. Shapiro and the PA Department of Health’s overbearing and unconstitutional proposed regulations is a tremendous victory for the grassroots efforts of Pennsylvanians. The people of Pennsylvania have been loud and clear in making their voices heard.
Together we worked to shine a spotlight on the 502-pages of massive Executive Branch overreach. Let me be clear – these proposed regulations should never have been pursued by the Shapiro Administration. From schools, to hospitals, to individual residences, the proposal sought to permit governmental oversight in almost every facet of one’s life, casting aside our Constitutional rights to privacy and unlawful searches and seizures.
This is a stark reminder that we must continue to be vigilant when the Executive Branch attempts overreach. We cannot and will not allow actions like we saw taken by the Executive Branch during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic to be put in place again. Protecting the freedoms and rights of Pennsylvanians remains of utmost importance for our Senate Republican Caucus.

SB 478 (FARRY)
Creates the Employee Ownership Assistance Program Act by establishing the Office of Employee Ownership within the Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) to serve as an advocate for improving government knowledge and support for profit-sharing and ownership stakes; increase awareness of how department programs affect companies with profit-sharing and ownership stake programs; and promote legislative or regulatory changes necessary to ensure that government policies encourage the adoption of existing and emerging profit-sharing programs. Establishes a program through which funding will be distributed to local administrative agencies for the purpose of providing low-interest loans to employee-ownership groups for technical assistance to develop or improve an employee-owned enterprise. Establishes a program through which funding will be distributed to local administrative agencies for the purpose of providing low-interest loans to employee-owned enterprises reorganizing industrial facilities, manufacturing facilities, and agricultural enterprises. Requires the Governor to appoint an employee ownership advocate who is qualified to represent the interest of employee-owned enterprises and will oversee the Office and the technical and financial assistance programs. Establishes the Employee Ownership Advisory Board to raise awareness for employee-owned
enterprises; research methods to encourage development and expansion of employee-owned enterprises; make recommendations to DCED and the General Assembly on policies related to employee-owned enterprises; develop proposed best practices for employee-owned enterprises; and develop educational materials and outreach opportunities for the maintenance and development of employee-owned enterprises.
PASSED 48-1
.
SB 980 (YAW)
Amends Title 35 (Health and Safety) to prohibit manufacturers from manufacturing or knowingly selling, offering for sale, or distributing for sale or use class B firefighting foam containing an intentionally added PFAS chemical that is not required under federal law. Prohibits the use of such foam, except for use by airports; chemical plants; oil refineries; flammable liquid, combustible liquid or natural gas terminals; or storage facilities, distribution facilities or electric generating facilities using natural gas. Establishes labeling, notification, and posting requirements on manufactures of personal protective equipment. Expands the use of Fire Company Grant Program funding to the disposal, transportation,
storage, and destruction of any unexpended stock of class B firefighting foam containing an intentionally added PFAS chemical, as well as the purchase or acquisition of class B firefighting foam that does not contain an intentionally added PFAS chemical. Allows the State Fire Commissioner to grant a waiver authorizing loans for the purchase of personal protective equipment containing intentionally added PFAS if it is determined that no viable or reasonable PFAS-free alternatives are available.
PASSED 48-1
.
SB 465 (LAUGHLIN)
Amends the Local Option Small Games of Chance Act to allow club licensees to retain 50% of the proceeds collected from eligible small games of chance, with the remaining 50% of the proceeds being paid for public interest purposes.

SB 1328 (BARTOLOTTA)
Creates the Utility Worksite Automated External Defibrillator (AED) Safety Act by requiring utilities to ensure at least one tested, maintained, and properly stored AED is readily available and operable at each worksite where linework or electrical work is performed for a utility. Exempts utilities that are responding to a mutual assistance event, such as an emergency or storm restoration. Requires utilities to communicate the location of each AED to workers at a worksite, provide AED and CPR training at no cost to workers, and ensure at least two workers at each worksite are trained in CPR and AED use. Provides Good Samaritan immunity to a person who renders emergency care with an AED. Authorizes the Department of Labor and Industry to investigate alleged violations and impose administrative penalties for violations.
PASSED 47-2
.

Amends the Sports Raffle Charities Act by requiring an affiliated nonprofit organization to remit five percent of the 50% total amount collected from the sale of athletic event drawing tickets to the Department of Revenue for donation to the Fire Company and the Emergency Medical Services Grant Programs. Requires each affiliated nonprofit organization to annually report to the State Treasurer for the prior year the total amount collected from drawing sales; the total amount donated to designated charitable organization or organizations for which a drawing was held; and the total amount remitted for the grant funding through the program. Welcoming Purchase Line Students to the Senate
I had the distinct honor and privilege of introducing a group of high school students from Purchase Line School District during Senate Session on Wednesday. The students were accompanied by their teacher, Mrs. Melinda Knapp.
I am a proud Purchase Line alumnus, and it was a great honor to welcome this group to the Pennsylvania Senate.
Pennsylvania Association of Boroughs
Thank you to Chris Yanoff for stopping by my office on Tuesday during his trip to the State Capitol.
Chris is the Manorville Borough Council President and Member of the Board of Directors of the Pennsylvania Association of Boroughs, representing Armstrong County. It was great to see him in Harrisburg, and I appreciated our discussion about local and state government issues!
Breast Cancer Awareness Month
The Capitol Fountain in Harrisburg has been turned pink in honor of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. It’s an annual reminder of our support and encouragement for those impacted by breast cancer.
Pennsylvania’s Act 1 of 2023 was a first-of-its-kind-in-the-nation comprehensive breast cancer screening bill, which was unanimously passed by the PA Senate and has been making a difference for the last three years. The legislation was introduced by Sens. Kim Ward, Devlin Robinson, and Tracy Pennycuick, who have all been tremendous advocates for improving lifesaving coverage.
Last year, thanks to the work of Sen. Frank Farry, we also passed Senate Bill 88 (Act 52 of 2025) to further update breast cancer screening coverage, building upon the work of Act 1, in order to help better diagnose, treat, and save the lives of those who will be affected by breast cancer.
Help us spread the word – Early Detection Saves Lives!
Senate Acts to Strengthen Property Rights
Property rights are enshrined in both the U.S. and the Pennsylvania constitutions, and the Senate approved legislation to strengthen protections against warrantless entry onto private property by Pennsylvania Game Commission personnel.
Senate Bill 1431
would require Game Commission personnel to obtain a valid warrant before entering private property, including posted land, unless a judicially recognized exception to the warrant requirement applies.
Current law gives Game Commission personnel broad authority to enter land outside buildings, whether posted or otherwise. Senate Bill 1431 would place clear limits on that authority while preserving recognized exceptions to the warrant requirement.
Read more about the effort to strengthen property rights
.
School Bus Driver Safety Bill Approved by Senate
Approximately 1.5 million children are transported on school buses every day in Pennsylvania, and the Senate approved legislation aimed at keeping reckless bus drivers from getting behind the wheel.
Senate Bill 1262
would increase penalties for school bus drivers who transport children while under the influence of alcohol, a controlled substance or a dangerous combination of both.
Read more about this school bus safety measure
.
The latest Senate action follows passage last year of
Senate Bill 65
, which would increase the required stopping distance for drivers approaching from the opposite direction when a school bus is stopped with its red lights flashing. Both bills await passage in the House of Representatives.
Senate Passes Bill to Establish Animal Abuser Registry
The Senate approved
Senate Bill 1311
, known as Aimee’s Law, to help prevent convicted abusers from obtaining more animals by establishing a statewide animal abuser registry. The bill was sent to the House of Representatives for consideration.
People selling, transferring or offering dogs, cats or horses for adoption would be required to check the registry, which would be maintained by Pennsylvania State Police, and refuse placement with anyone listed. These requirements will help shelters, rescues and others placing animals in new homes identify convicted abusers before another animal is put at risk.
The legislation is named after a six-month-old husky found abandoned in a crate beneath a bridge in Erie during subzero temperatures. She was severely underweight, covered in filth and suffering from frostbite on all four paws. Despite the rescuers’ efforts to save her, Aimee did not survive.
Read more about Aimee’s Law
.

Gov. Josh Shapiro’s Department of Health (DOH) withdrew proposed health regulations that would have vastly expanded state government’s power over the lives of Pennsylvanians, a tremendous victory for the grassroots efforts of commonwealth citizens.
Shortly before the regulations were withdrawn, more than 10,000 citizens, school officials and others submitted comments to the Independent Regulatory Review Commission expressing their serious concerns. I joined my colleagues in a

The proposed regulations would have given the state more power to enter homes and businesses without a warrant, speak to students without parents present, access private health records, unilaterally impose mask mandates and more. The DOH introduced the massive, 502-page regulatory overhaul without input from the public or the General Assembly.
Although these regulations were withdrawn, we must remain vigilant – the governor’s DOH could resubmit them at any time.

The measure also received bipartisan support in both the Senate and House, was signed into law by Democrat Governor Josh Shapiro and was supported by SEPTA.
“The lawlessness perpetuated by District Attorney Larry Krasner has been detrimental to the safety of America’s 6th largest city. However, since Act 40 was fully implemented, we have seen greater stability for riders and employees across the SEPTA network, along with a decline in crime. Remembering 9/11 25 Years Later
On Sept. 11, 2001, terrorists highjacked four airliners on America’s east coast and turned them into deadly missiles, ultimately taking the lives of nearly 3,000 citizens in the name of Islamic fundamentalism.
Filled with passengers, two of the planes were flown into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and another into the Pentagon in Washington, D.C.  The fourth, perhaps destined to strike the White House or U.S. Capitol, was brought down in Somerset County by brave passengers who fought back.
Twenty-five years later, we recall the shock and anger over the attack, the grief over lives taken and the resolve to prevent another act of that scale. I hope we also remember the nation coming together in response, and the power of a unified people facing adversity. As the number of people who experienced this event declines, it becomes more important to dedicate ourselves to never letting that day slip from our nation’s memory.
Protecting Children and Families from AI Deception
It’s critical for state laws to keep up with fast-evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, especially as it relates to protecting our children online. I’m proud of our work to address the alarming rise in AI-generated sexual images of children, as well as non-consenting adults, through

Working to Increase Affordability for Pennsylvanians
At a time when families continue to feel the strain of inflation, we know state government must look for ways to implement policies and programs to increase affordability. Fighting for the state budget to respect taxpayers and take less of your hard-earned money, enacting the Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit and the Employer Child Care Contribution Tax Credit Programs, and making homes more attainable are some of the ways we’ve focused on affordability during the 2025-26 legislative session.
The new
Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit
provides meaningful relief for working families across the commonwealth. Families that claim the federal Earned Income Tax Credit may also claim the state tax credit equal to 10% of the federal amount. This amounts to hundreds of dollars saved every year for many working families.
We also created the
Employer Child Care Contribution Tax Credit Program
, which provides incentives for businesses to make contributions of up to $500 annually toward their employees’ child-care costs.
And we took steps to
make housing attainable
to more Pennsylvanians by passing legislation streamlining municipal approval processes, reducing delays, cutting unnecessary red tape, and creating a Housing Development Regulatory Compliance Officer to serve as a single point of contact and improve coordination in the permitting process.
We’re committed to continuing to implement greater government efficiencies and policies to control the growth of spending and help address affordability for families throughout Pennsylvania.
Key Election Dates to Remember
Election Day will be here before you know it, and I want to make sure you know the key dates.
The first step is registering to vote, and the deadline to do that is Monday, Oct. 19.
If you want to vote by absentee ballot, the deadline to file a request is Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
To make sure you’re registered, learn how to request an absentee ballot and find your polling place, visit the
state’s elections information webpage
.
New Law Cracks Down on Robocalls, Scam Texts and Caller ID Spoofing
Legislation we unanimously passed enacting stronger protections from deceptive telemarketing practices will take effect Monday, Oct. 19.
Under
Act 47 of 2026
, Pennsylvania’s telemarketing law will now cover modern forms of solicitation, including text messages, voicemails, ringless voicemails and robocalls. It also establishes stronger rules for when and how telemarketers can contact Pennsylvanians, including:
Prohibiting telemarketing calls before 9 a.m. and after 7 p.m. and on Sundays.
Requiring prior express written consent for most robocalls and telemarketing text messages.
Prohibiting telemarketers from falsely identifying themselves or using deceptive caller ID information, including spoofed numbers.
Requiring telemarketers to stop a solicitation when a consumer asks them to do so.
The legislation also prohibits the use of AI-generated messages to deceive consumers.

Homer-Center School District
has advanced in the T-Mobile Friday Night Lights contest and they are now competing for one of four $250,000 prizes plus a full Gronk weight room, with a chance to move on for a $1,000,000 field renovation.

National Prescription Drug Take Back Day is Oct. 24
According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, most people who use prescription medication for a nonmedical purpose obtained that medication from a family member or friend. Removing unnecessary medications from the home can help remove this risk.
National Prescription Drug Take Back Day is Oct. 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., providing a safe, convenient and responsible means of disposing of prescription drugs.

.

Metastatic breast cancer, also known as Stage IV breast cancer, is diagnosed when breast cancer has spread to other parts of the body. While treatments can help control metastatic cancer and allow many people to live longer, Stage IV breast cancer is currently considered incurable.

Great News! I’m pleased to join with Rep. Jim Struzzi and Rep. Jill Cooper to announce two area projects are receiving funding through the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority (PENNVEST).
Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County
The Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County was awarded a total of $10 million – $5.39 million in grant funding and a $4.6 million low-interest loan – to replace 1,000 residential lead service lines in Avonmore and Oklahoma boroughs, and Bell, Unity, Hempfield, Loyalhanna and Salem townships. The approval of funding for this project will save the affected households from an expected 112% user fee increase.
Blairsville Municipal Authority
A grant of $2,501,213 and low interest loan of $93,787 has been approved for the Blairsville Municipal Authority. The funding will be used for Phase 1 of a lead service line replacement project. The project includes replacement of approximately 122 service connections consisting of galvanized pipe formerly attached to, and located downstream of, water mains containing lead goosenecks and other lead components. The work encompasses associated excavation, backfill, and restoration. Of the 122 service connections, 115 are located in the Borough of Blairsville, and seven are located in Burrell Township.
Aging waterlines are problems for communities throughout Pennsylvania, as they are expensive to maintain. I am pleased the substantial funding approved by PENNVEST will provide support for critical work to improve water quality and ensure the continued health and safety of local residents.
PENNVEST financing is provided through the use of federal funding and prior bond issues by the state as well as proceeds from the Marcellus Shale Impact Fee legislation, Act 13 of 2012.
Western PA School for the Deaf
It was a pleasure to visit with Carson Granado during his visit to the State Capitol for a tour and to see the Senate in session. He is from the Apollo area and is a student at the Western PA School for the Deaf. This is the second time I have had the chance to meet with Carson during a Capitol visit. He enjoys math and aspires to be an aerospace engineer.
Thank you to Carson, his classmates, and teachers for taking the time to travel to Harrisburg!
Fighting for Affordable Energy
Rising energy costs have put added pressure on Pennsylvania families and businesses and must be addressed. This legislative session, I made it a priority to prevent new energy taxes and support energy development that strengthens reliability and helps bring costs down.
As part of the 2025-26 budget agreement, I worked with my colleagues to eliminate Pennsylvania’s participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) – a multi-state pact that would have added more than a billion dollars in new electricity taxes.
I also supported Senate passage of legislation eliminating the gross receipts tax on electric bills, which would save ratepayers more than $1.7 billion over the first year. Unfortunately, the House of Representatives never approved the tax cut we added to
House Bill 1667
.
Because lack of energy development drives up costs, the Senate passed legislation to reduce Pennsylvania’s electric generation shortfall and expand energy development.
Senate Bill 704
directs the state departments of Community and Economic Development and Environmental Protection to work together to identify suitable sites for natural gas electric generation projects. The House also failed to act on this measure.
I will continue fighting for lower energy prices, supporting policies which will cut your costs.

It was great to spend some time at
Two Lick Valley Social Center
recently. I appreciated the warm welcome and I was pleased to bring ornaments made at the center with me to Harrisburg! The ornaments will be part of the Christmas tree decorations at the State Capitol.

PA House Needs to Act to Protect Pennsylvania Communities
In March, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled the state’s mandatory life-without-parole sentence for second-degree murder is unconstitutional. The court gave the General Assembly until July 24 to enact a new rule. The Senate passed legislation to protect our communities and fix the problem – twice.
Instead of acting on our bipartisan
Senate Bill 1400
, the House of Representatives advanced a proposal tied to expanding medical parole, creating additional opportunities – without proper guardrails – for convicted felons to be released before completing their sentences.
Senate Bill 1400 is supported by Attorney General Dave Sunday, PA State Lodge FOP, PA State Troopers Association and district attorneys across the commonwealth. It has languished in the House Judiciary Committee since June. Second‑degree murder is an extremely serious crime, and the House needs to act so these criminals remain behind bars.
New Law Means PA Schools Will Be Cellphone-Free
Pennsylvania teachers will no longer have to compete with smartphones for their students’ attention – and kids will be able to get through the school day without the constant pressure of social media and notifications – with bipartisan passage of a new law requiring schools to adopt policies prohibiting student cellphone use during the school day.
Act 117 of 2026
includes limited exceptions, such as students with individualized education plans and special occasions such as field days. It establishes a clear statewide standard, while allowing school districts, which have direct contact with parents, to decide what works best for their communities.
The law will take effect with the 2027-28 school year. Pennsylvania joins 40 states in restricting these devices – 19 of which have school-day bans.

Obtaining justice for sexual assault survivors requires timely processing of rape kit evidence, and I joined colleagues in making it a priority to improve and standardize rape kit testing.
Previously, state law allowed local law enforcement agencies to determine whether a sexual assault evidence kit should undergo DNA testing or other forensic analysis, creating the potential for inconsistent practices across the commonwealth. We passed a new law eliminating such discretion.
